paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, “Still, it is better than being conventional.” Meitei was simply taking the master’s side in everything. The master’s wife, apparently rather dissatisfied, said, “Then I should like to ask you gentlemen something. You are forever saying ‘conventional, conventional,’ but what exactly do you mean by ‘conventional’?” The master’s wife had now quite seriously begun asking for a definition of “conventional.” “You ask what ‘conventional’ is? Well, ‘conventional’ is rather hard to explain...” “If it is so vague that you cannot explain it, would it not be better not to speak of ‘conventional’ at all?” The master’s wife pressed him hard with that peculiar feminine logic. “It is not vague. I understand it perfectly; it is merely difficult to explain.” “I suppose you call anything you dislike ‘conventional.’” The master’s wife had unconsciously hit upon the truth. At this point Meitei had no choice but to dispose of the matter of “conventionality” somehow. “Madam Kushami, by ‘conventional’ I mean fellows who lie about in melancholy reverie, pining day and night for some young beauty, sick with love; or those people who, whenever the weather clears, invariably take a flask of wine and go strolling along the Sumida embankment.” The master’s wife could not understand what Meitei meant, so she gave the vague reply, “Are there really such people?” Then she added, “It is all so muddled that I cannot make it out.” In the end she had no choice but to abandon the questioning. Meitei said, “To give another example: attach the head of Major Pendennis to Bakin’s body, then wrap the whole thing for a year or two in the air of Europe, and you will have it about right.” The master’s wife said, “If one did that, would it count as ‘conventional’?” Meitei only smiled and did not answer, then went on, “In fact, you need not go to such trouble to produce the conventional. Add a Shirokiya head clerk to a middle-school student and divide by two, and you will get a perfectly respectable specimen of the conventional.” The master’s wife tilted her head, still looking unconvinced, and said, “Is that so?”

paragraphs.source_en: “What, are you still here?” The master, who had returned before anyone noticed, sat down beside Meitei and said this. “What do you mean, ‘still here’! When you left, did you not tell me, ‘I’ll be right back, so please wait’?” said Meitei. The master’s wife looked at Meitei and said, “You see, that is just the sort of man he is!” Meitei said to Kushami, “While you were out, I was privileged to hear every last anecdote about you.” The master said, “Women are always too talkative; it is the worst thing about them. If only people would keep silent, like this cat.” As he spoke, the master stroked my head. Meitei said, “I hear you even fed grated daikon to the baby.” The master laughed with a little “hmm” and then said, “Even if she is a baby, babies these days are really clever. Since then, whenever I ask her, ‘Baby, where is it hot?’ she sticks out her tongue. It is quite amusing.” Meitei said, “That is just like teaching tricks to a puppy; it is cruel.” Then, as if suddenly remembering, he said, “By the way, Kangetsu ought to be arriving soon.” The master asked, puzzled, “Is Kangetsu coming?” Meitei said, “He is coming. I sent him a postcard telling him to come to Kushami’s house by one o’clock this afternoon.” “You really do take matters into your own hands without asking whether it suits me. What business do you have in making Kangetsu come here?” “No particular business. Today’s idea was not mine; it was Kangetsu’s own request. The fellow is apparently going to give a lecture at the Physical Society, and he wanted me to listen while he rehearsed it. I said, ‘Excellent, let Kushami hear it too,’ and told him to come to your house. You have nothing to do anyway, so it is just right, is it not? In any case it will not inconvenience you, so you may as well listen to him.” In this way Meitei settled the matter on the master’s behalf. The master, seeming somewhat displeased with Meitei’s high-handedness, said, “I would not understand a lecture on physics.” Meitei said, “But Kangetsu’s subject is not some dry and tasteless matter such as magnetized nozzles. His title is the extraordinary and unworldly ‘The Mechanics of Hanging,’ so it is well worth hearing.” The master said, “Since you once tried to hang yourself and failed, it may be worth your hearing, but as for me...” Meitei replied with his usual banter, “Even a man who gets chills at the Kabuki-za cannot be conclusively said unfit to listen.” The master’s wife laughed softly, glanced at the master, and withdrew to the next room. The master silently stroked my head; only at such times did he stroke me with extraordinary gentleness.
